blocks.text: An MCP server that only runs on your laptop is not much use to a team.
Kubernetes takes a packaged container and keeps it running reliably, at scale, across machines.
This lesson covers packaging, deploying, health checks, and safe rolling updates for an MCP server.
1. Why Kubernetes for an MCP Server

blocks.alt: A Deployment manages three Pods behind a single stable Service

blocks.text: An MCP server is just a process that talks to clients over HTTP or another transport.
Kubernetes takes care of restarting it when it crashes, running several copies, and rolling out new versions.
None of that is MCP specific. Kubernetes only sees a container, not what is inside it.
You describe the desired state, and Kubernetes continuously works to make reality match it.

blocks.title: One requirement first
blocks.content: Kubernetes runs containers, so your MCP server needs a container image before any of this applies.

blocks.text: 2. Packaging the Server as a Container
The starting point is a normal container image, built with a Dockerfile, same as any other service.
The image should expose an HTTP port and read configuration from environment variables, not from files baked into it.

code.content:
FROM node:20-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

blocks.text: Once this builds and runs locally with docker run, it is ready to push to a registry Kubernetes can pull from.
3. Pods, the Smallest Deployable Unit

blocks.alt: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit running a container

blocks.text: A Pod is the smallest thing Kubernetes schedules, and it usually wraps a single container.
Pods are disposable. Kubernetes can kill one and start a fresh one at any time.
Because of this, your MCP server should not keep important state only inside its own Pod.
4. The Deployment Manifest

blocks.alt: A Deployment manifest defines Pods while a Service manifest defines how to reach them

blocks.text: A Deployment describes how many copies of your Pod should exist and how to roll out changes to them.
You rarely write a bare Pod by hand. A Deployment manages Pods for you instead.

code.content:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: weather-mcp
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: weather-mcp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: weather-mcp
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: weather-mcp
          image: registry.example.com/weather-mcp:1.4.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "250m"
              memory: "256Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: "512Mi"

blocks.text: The replicas field is the whole mechanism behind running more than one copy of your server.
Changing it from one to three is the entire act of horizontal scaling, no code changes needed.
5. The Service Manifest
Every time a Pod restarts, it gets a new internal address, so nothing can depend on that address directly.
A Service gives a single, stable address that always points at whichever Pods are currently healthy.

code.content:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: weather-mcp
spec:
  selector:
    app: weather-mcp
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
  type: ClusterIP

blocks.text: A ClusterIP Service is only reachable inside the cluster, which fits an internal MCP server well.
6. Labels Tie Everything Together
A Service does not know how a Pod was created. It only matches Pods by their labels.
This is why the Deployment and the Service both use app: weather-mcp in the manifests above.

blocks.text: 7. Liveness Probes

blocks.alt: A liveness probe is compared against a readiness probe

blocks.text: A liveness probe answers one question, is this container stuck and should it be restarted.
If it keeps failing, Kubernetes kills the container and starts a new one in its place.

code.content:
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 10

blocks.text: The health endpoint should be cheap and simple, just confirming the process is alive, nothing more.
8. Readiness Probes
A readiness probe answers a different question, is this container ready to receive real traffic right now.
A failed readiness probe removes the Pod from the Service, no restart happens.

code.content:
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /ready
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 2
  periodSeconds: 5

blocks.title: Readiness and liveness are not the same
blocks.content: Readiness controls traffic routing. Liveness controls restarts. Mixing them up causes confusing outages.

blocks.text: 9. Combining Probes in One Manifest
In practice both probes live together inside the same container spec, right next to resources.

code.content:
containers:
  - name: weather-mcp
    image: registry.example.com/weather-mcp:1.4.0
    ports:
      - containerPort: 8080
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 2
      periodSeconds: 5
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /health
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10

blocks.text: With both in place, Kubernetes finally knows the difference between running and actually ready to serve.
10. Rolling Updates

blocks.alt: A rolling update replaces old Pods with new ones a few at a time

blocks.text: Updating the image field on a Deployment triggers a rolling update automatically, no extra command needed.
Kubernetes starts new Pods, waits for each to pass its readiness probe, then retires an old Pod.
This repeats until every Pod runs the new version, and the Service never drops to zero ready Pods.

code.content:
kubectl set image deployment/weather-mcp weather-mcp=registry.example.com/weather-mcp:1.5.0
kubectl rollout status deployment/weather-mcp

blocks.text: 11. Controlling the Pace of a Rollout
Two settings control exactly how a rolling update proceeds, maxSurge and maxUnavailable.
maxSurge allows extra Pods above the replica count during the update. maxUnavailable allows some to be down.

code.content:
spec:
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0

blocks.text: Setting maxUnavailable to zero guarantees full capacity is kept throughout the whole update.
12. Rolling Back a Bad Deploy

blocks.alt: A bad rollout is rolled back to the previous Deployment revision

blocks.text: If a new version turns out to be broken, undoing it is just as mechanical as rolling it out.
Kubernetes keeps a history of previous Deployment revisions specifically for this purpose.

code.content:
kubectl rollout undo deployment/weather-mcp
kubectl rollout history deployment/weather-mcp

blocks.text: A rollback is itself just another rolling update, moving back to the last known good image.
13. Watching a Deployment in Practice
A handful of commands answer almost every question about whether a rollout is actually healthy.

code.content:
kubectl get pods -l app=weather-mcp
kubectl describe pod weather-mcp-7d9f8c6b5-xk2pl
kubectl logs weather-mcp-7d9f8c6b5-xk2pl --previous

blocks.text: The previous flag on logs shows output from before a crash, often the only place the real error is visible.
14. Resource Requests and Limits

blocks.alt: A resource request is compared against a resource limit

blocks.text: Requests tell the scheduler how much CPU and memory a Pod needs, to decide which node has room.
Limits cap how much a Pod can actually use, so one runaway process cannot starve its neighbors.

items: requests set the minimum a Pod is guaranteed for scheduling purposes.
limits.memory being exceeded gets a Pod killed with an out of memory error.
limits.cpu being exceeded only throttles the Pod, it is not killed.

blocks.text: Worked Example: A Complete Deployment
Here is everything from this lesson combined into one minimal, working set of manifests.

code.content:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: kb-mcp
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: kb-mcp }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: kb-mcp }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: kb-mcp
          image: registry.example.com/kb-mcp:1.0.0
          ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi" }
            limits: { cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi" }
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: kb-mcp
spec:
  selector: { app: kb-mcp }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]

blocks.text: Applying this and watching kubectl get pods confirms the whole chain works end to end.
Once all three Pods show Running and Ready, the Service is already load balancing across them.
Common Mistakes

items: Deploying without resource requests or limits, leaving one bad Pod free to starve a whole node.
Confusing readiness and liveness, causing Kubernetes to restart Pods that are just busy, not broken.
Running only one replica, so a single Pod restart becomes a full outage.
Skipping kubectl rollout status and assuming a deploy worked the moment apply returns.
Setting maxUnavailable too high, letting a bad rollout take down most of your capacity at once.

blocks.text: Practice
Take a container you have already built and write a Deployment and Service for it, using this lesson as a template.

code.content:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f service.yaml
kubectl scale deployment kb-mcp --replicas=4
kubectl get pods -l app=kb-mcp -w

blocks.text: Then deploy an intentionally broken image and watch the Service keep routing only to still healthy Pods.
Key Takeaway
A Deployment and Service turn a single container image into a self healing, updatable service.
Health probes tell Kubernetes when a Pod is truly ready, and rolling updates use that to deploy safely with zero downtime.
